BOTTLENECK SUMMARY: for the workload(s) non-stream, stream the gateway IS the limit at the top concurrency, so those throughput figures do reflect gateway cost rather than only the mock's ceiling.

CLIENT-BOUND PHASES: at least one phase shows a client-observed mean more than twice the gateway's own recorded mean, i.e. most of the wall clock was spent inside the load generator rather than the gateway (cmd\loadtest prints a warning of its own in this case). Those phases measure this client, not the gateway: gateway/stream/c128: client-observed mean 45.604ms vs gateway mean 15.0546ms; gateway-scraped/non-stream/c128: client-observed mean 31.7452ms vs gateway mean 14.6593ms; gateway-scraped/stream/c128: client-observed mean 45.9797ms vs gateway mean 15.1528ms; horizontal-2/stream/c128: client-observed mean 44.2148ms vs gateway mean 15.0328ms; horizontal-4/stream/c128: client-observed mean 45.6275ms vs gateway mean 15.0654ms; second/non-stream/c128: client-observed mean 28.7712ms vs gateway mean 13.9614ms; second/stream/c128: client-observed mean 43.8165ms vs gateway mean 14.7747ms; traced-full/non-stream/c128: client-observed mean 33.6349ms vs gateway mean 15.1536ms

HOST NOISE: every figure is the median of 3 interleaved rounds, and the per-round QPSMin/QPSMax are in the rows so the spread is visible. Rounds are outermost (all 8 arms run once per round) so drift hits the arms alike, but the host was also running this script, 6 gateway instances, a mock and a collector throughout.
Everything is loopback on ONE host. There is no network in the path, so no figure here includes transport cost, and the five gateway instances compete for the same CPU, memory bus and loopback stack.

LOG LEVEL: the gateways run at log level 'error' so that per-request logging is NOT mixed into the tracing cost. configs\observability.yaml documents that info-level per-request logging costs about 18% QPS and 4ms P95 at concurrency 32 on this host -- that cost is not measured here.

EXPORTERS ARE ASYNCHRONOUS: both sinks own a background worker and Export() only enqueues, so the number measured is the cost of building and enqueueing a span tree (plus sink-worker contention), not the cost of a synchronous write. A slow or unreachable collector delays delivery and grows the drop counter; it does not block the request path.

Tracing is enabled per INSTANCE at sample_ratio 1.0, so every request in the traced arms produced a trace. The traced arms therefore show the worst case for the tracing layer, not a sampled deployment.

The 4-instance arm (ports 18999, 19000, 19001, 19002) is the same shape as the repo's documented infergate-fleet Prometheus scrape job, which targets 127.0.0.1:18999-19002 as four identical instances behind one mock upstream. This host reports 24 physical cores / 32 logical processors, so the 4-instance arm is not core-starved -- but a single host is still a single host, so linearity measured here is an upper bound on what these instances cost each other, not a cluster result.

A `direct` arm that is as fast as the `gateway` arm does NOT mean the gateway is free: it means this harness cannot see the gateway's ceiling through this backend. The tracing arms are the ones that still produce a usable relative signal in that regime, because they change what the gateway does rather than how much the backend can absorb.

SCRAPE LOAD is an UPPER BOUND, not a Prometheus model: the gateway-scraped arm holds a constant 100ms poll of /stats + /metrics for the whole arm, whereas a real Prometheus scrapes every 5-15s. It answers 'what does being scraped cost' in the most aggressive regime this harness can produce, not what a normal scrape interval costs.

SCRAPE RATE CEILING: the scrape arm ASKS for a 10 endpoint-GETs/s poll (one GET to each of /stats + /metrics every 100ms). The co-located scraper is a PowerShell loop invoking curl.exe, whose process-spawn cost caps it at ~9.702 endpoint GETs/s (0.9702x intended, per-round 9.911/9.599/9.601, spread 3.25% -- stable, so a systematic ceiling rather than flakiness). That is still about 48.5x a 5s Prometheus scrape interval, so the scrape-cost delta in this artifact is an UPPER BOUND for a real Prometheus, not a model of one -- and part of the delta is the scraper process competing for the same cores.

The scraper in the SCRAPE LOAD arm is a PowerShell background job (curl.exe in a loop) on the SAME host and the SAME CPU as the gateway it scrapes, so part of any gateway-scraped-vs-gateway delta is the scraper process competing for cores rather than the exposition code getting slower. Read that delta as the cost of being scraped by a co-located scraper, which is the worst case a Prometheus deployment would present.
